transcript.text: Welcome to Straightforward, a podcast about Taiwan, the island at the center of technological
innovation and the global fight for democracy. I'm your host Channing Lee and I'm here in Taipei. I'm
really excited to have a conversation about a topic that we've talked a little bit about,
but not in too much depth, and that is civilian defense. As you know from all of
our conversations, Taiwan faces a plethora of threats from Beijing. But those threats
don't stop at traditional military coercion. Disinformation, information manipulation,
cognitive warfare, psychological manipulation, legal intimidation, transnational repression.
These are all ways in which Beijing is trying to start a war with Taiwan before a war even starts.
And in that sense, it's really important for us to understand how Taiwan has been mobilizing people,
reaching out to civilians, to citizens to get them thinking about how to prepare in
case of a crisis. On that note, I'm really honored today to be joined by legislator
Puma Shen. He is a national leader in all these conversations around civilian
preparedness and he's now a legislator in the legislative br. Puma is the founder of double
think lab of Kuma Academy and a professor at NTEU. So I'm really really excited to
have this conversation with him and join me in welcoming him to straightforward. [music]
Legislator Shan Puma, thank you so much for having me, having us here at your office. We really
appreciate you. My pleasure. Taking the time to join Straight Forward. So welcome to Straight
Forward. [laughter] Thanks. Hi everyone. I think um you've had such an amazing and inspiring career
and before we get into all the substance I do want to ask if you can introduce yourself
you know you started as a criminologist [clears throat] and to you founded a lot of civil society
initiatives from double think lab to kum academy and and now you're in the ly so we'll talk through
all that today but wonder if you [clears throat] can just introduce yourself to our audience okay
so my name is Pumash I'm the associate professor from national Taipei University and I'm also the
legislator here in our legislative ATVM here in Taiwan. And here in Taiwan is a little
different. I mean, you still keep your position at a university. So, I still have to teach like
two courses per week. Yeah. But I raise my salary here from [laughter] I mean for the ne still for
the next two years. I see. [laughter] So, what inspired you initially to advocate for civil
resilience? Mhm. I think uh because I was a lawyer before actually and I graduated from law school
here and also from University of Pennsylvania and uh mostly I mean uh it's all about like
criminal criminal cases. So actually you have to visit prison like pretty often and then you
have to I mean talk and interview with lots of criminals and you can actually feel the vibe. I
mean to really know that there's like minorities here uh in our society that's pretty suffered I
mean from not just the legal system but I mean got all the pressure I mean from economy from
all kind of resources so I think that's the time when I joined lots of like grassroot movements
and care about human rights and so for my PhD I studied a lot about white collar crime because I
I mean I feel like there are lots of criminals but they are actually having some privilege
and not being invest stigated. So I studied a lot about financial crime and state crime. And

or or China or Iran and then we are debunking all this together so you won't be I mean killed
when infiltrate one by one so I mean all these authorized states are collaborating with each
other right now. We need to collaborate with each other right now also. Yeah. Now we've at SCSP,
you know, we write extensively about this axis of disruptors, right? China, North Korea, Iran,
right? They're all working, Russia, all working together to kind of spread these narratives. So,
I'm really glad that obviously Taiwan is defending itself in this fight, but hopefully also,
you know, working with allies and partners on this piece. Yeah. So, I know you're a really
busy guy. I don't want to spend too much time. Are there any kind of legislative priorities for 2026
that you're looking forward to? I know that the defense budget is still um up in the air. That's
the thing. I mean the one of the narratives that they always want to spread is that you
vote for DPP the ruling party you're voting for the battlefield you're I mean you're be on the
battlefield and that's how they try to scare our own citizen and that's how they said if we talk
with China we don't need all these defense budget but I don't believe that's the case I mean China
will not keep any promise you never talk with China and then if you really talk with them and
sign a peace agreement the last region that signed a peace agreement is Tibet we do not want to be
Tibetan in the future we do not want to be Hong come I mean all these I mean cases are just in
front of us and that's the message we really want to tell the public but that's hard like I said not
everyone cares about national security so I often I mean deliver the speech in the university or
even just I mean hold a microphone on the street I mean talking to our citizen right hey this is the
danger that we're we're facing that please I mean support us and please support not our party but
support this nation I mean even we have different opinions among all these parties we should be on
the same website where you talk where we talk about digital security and national digital
defense. Well, thank you so much for your time. My pleasure. The last thing we always asked all
of our guests uh you know the one of the purposes of straightforward as [clears throat] a podcast is
to help our audiences in DC and around the world get to know Taiwan a little bit more. Obviously,
we talk a lot about some of these more serious topics. We have some more fun topics as well. Um I
like to ask our guests at the end of each episode if you had a recommendation for Taiwan. could be
a book, a movie, a food, something that um you know, if you don't know anything about Taiwan,
somebody like to help introduce you to Taiwan. What would your recommendation be and why? First,
I think we have great food. I mean, we often talk about food. We have like boba tea. I mean,
I mean, it's very famous, but I think also I mean come to Taiwan when during the election
would be very great because election is more like sports here in Taiwan. [laughter] So you could see
like lots of political talk shows and lots of festival and you know maybe the a week or two
weeks before the election I mean people would be on the street and I mean there are so many things
I mean we got lots of parade and that's actually a really good recommendation. Yeah. So so I it's

I really appreciate you joining Straight Forward. Thank you. Thank you so much. [music] Thanks.

for explaining all the efforts that he and others in Taiwan are working on in
order to bolster civilian defense. I found it so fascinating the way that he explained
cognitive warfare. Um, he's a professor, so obviously he's good at explaining things. Um,
but I think one thing that he stressed that I really want to come back to is that
cognitive warfare is not necessarily just about spreading information, whether false or real,
right? It's actually about trying to shape public opinion. You know, from Beijing's perspective,
cognitive warfare is deployed in Taiwan in order to sway people's opinions of Beijing, of the CCP,
and of what they're trying to do. And that is actually a really, really dangerous tool that
um has proven that the war has perhaps already begun in the minds of the CCP. Understanding
cognitive warfare and how Beijing is deploying that against people in Taiwan and around the world
is really important because I think that question about Taiwan's will to fight is one that we think
a lot about in the United States. So understanding how external factors are now influencing Taiwan's
will to fight is actually really important to understanding some of the ways in which people are
thinking about their future here in Taiwan. Puma is extremely brave. I don't want to underemphasize
